title: Monastrell in Spain
subtitle: Power in the south-east
objectives: Explain how heat and drought shape it

steps.title: Jumilla, Yecla, Alicante
steps.body: In Spain, Monastrell dominates the hot, dry south-east. Jumilla, Yecla and Alicante are its main DOs. Vineyards sit at 400 to 800 m on poor, limestone soils, often as old bush vines, many ungrafted because phylloxera struggles in sandy soils. Rainfall is low, often 300 mm a year.
steps.highlight: Old bush vines in the dry south-east

steps.title: Heat and drought
steps.body: The heat gives ripe, dark fruit and high alcohol, often 14.5 to 15.5%. Drought keeps berries small and concentrated. Altitude brings cooler nights, preserving some freshness. Once known for bulk wines, these regions now make concentrated reds at good prices, and some powerful, oaked premium wines.

steps.prompt: Why are many Monastrell vines in south-east Spain ungrafted?
steps.explanation: Sandy soils make it hard for phylloxera to move, so some old vines grow on their own roots.

steps.title: Sweet Fondillón
steps.body: Alicante also makes Fondillón, a historic sweet wine from overripe Monastrell, fermented naturally and aged for at least 10 years in old casks, often in a solera. It reaches 16 to 18% alcohol without fortification. It was famous in the 17th and 18th centuries and is now a protected rarity.

steps.prompt: Match each Spanish term to its meaning.
steps.explanation: South-east Spain is Monastrell's home ground.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Jumilla, Yecla and Alicante are Monastrell's heartland
Heat and drought give ripe, dark, powerful reds
Fondillón is Alicante's historic aged sweet wine
